On Euronews' first edition of Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones led a debate on Europe's latest migration crackdown, after five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants.

In the first edition of Euronews' new flagship show, Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones brought viewers the latest analysis of the stories making headlines over the weekend and on Monday.

Jones opened the programme with the latest EU developments on migration, as five countries - Greece, Denmark, Germany, Austria and the Netherlands - announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants, with the first pilot centres expected to be operational by mid-2027.

Our correspondent Vincenzo Genovese, reporting from Vienna, said it marked an unprecedented move in EU migration policy, with the bloc sending irregular migrants to a country with which they have no previous connection - a move compared to Donald Trump's approach in the US.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the agreement a "game changer," saying it would help European countries regain control and remove incentives for illegal migrants.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, the first facility will accommodate around 100 people. The hub would consist of open facilities rather than closed deportation centres, and migrants would be free to move around the country. The goal is to give them the chance to integrate into local society and the labour market.

The EU law enabling return hubs outside the bloc states that only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards are respected” are eligible.

Rwanda has a questionable track record on human rights. However, Rwanda's minister of the interior, Vincent Biruta, said the country was ready, had good experience in dealing with migrants and would respect fundamental rights.

Legal challenges could emerge when deportations begin next year, as happened with the UK-Rwanda agreement.

On Monday, Frederiksen added that she had a strong feeling that other countries would join the scheme.

Nineteen of the twenty-seven EU governments support the deportation plan. Only France and Spain have made clear their opposition to it. Italy already has its own agreement with Albania.

THE DEBATE

MEPs Charlie Weimers and Abir Al-Sahlani discuss Rwanda

Jones hosted Swedish MEP Charlie Weimers, a Member of the European Parliament since 2019 and part of the European Conservatives and Reformists group, and Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of the Renew Europe Group, who has also been an MEP since 2019, to debate the Rwanda "Return Hub."

Weimers said he agreed with Frederiksen, adding that he thought the policy was a "game changer." Noting that "every system" starts small, he said it would be successful if it led to further steps in the future to address migration policy in the EU.

Al-Sahlani pondered the feasibility of Rwanda returning migrants to their countries of origin, questioning how Rwanda would be able to carry out such returns when European countries themselves had struggled to do so.

“If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked, citing concerns over Rwanda's dependence on development aid and security concerns, as well as other unanswered questions.

Weimers calls deal a 'deterrent'

Meanwhile, Jones challenged Weimers over the cost-effectiveness of the proposed centres, citing Italy’s Albania scheme, which is costing Italian taxpayers €670 million over five years while handling only 0.3% of illegal arrivals into Italy. But Weimers described the new deal as being intended as a "deterrent" to those considering illegally migrating to Europe.

Al-Sahlani also criticised the growing influence of far-right narratives on European migration policy, arguing that governments were failing to use existing legislation and tools effectively.

The Renew Europe Group MEP further accused political leaders of portraying refugees as a threat and making them scapegoats for wider societal problems. She also warned that migration debates were increasingly driven by emotion rather than facts, fuelled by the misuse of statistics, selective truths and fabricated stories that vilify people seeking refuge.

Under new rules, public bodies such as municipalities and towns are to be generally liable for VAT when they engage in commercial activities.

Controversy is brewing in Germany over the country's so-called "bratwurst tax."

From 1 January, new VAT rules are set to apply across all German municipalities, potentially meaning that key local community groups such as volunteer fire brigades could have to pay tax on sales of things such as bratwursts at village festivals and other local events.

The changes stem from section 2b of Germany's VAT Act, which has been repeatedly delayed but which is now expected to come into force. Under the rules, public bodies such as municipalities and towns are to be generally liable for VAT when they engage in commercial activities.

That means if a volunteer fire brigade operates as part of the municipality and not as an independent association, VAT would have to be paid on sales at local events.

Since 1 January 2026, a reduced tax rate of 7% has applied to food sold at snack bars or in restaurants. However, those affected have to keep detailed records of their sales and issue receipts.

On the website "Kommunal.de," Christian Erhardt-Maciejewski has taken a satirical swipe at the tax in a piece titled "Hurrah, the tax office is grilling the fire brigade."

He writes: "I can already imagine what will happen now: the most resourceful brigades will set up a support association so that they can carry on selling sausages. The fire brigade festival becomes an association festival, the grill master turns into a treasurer, mustard becomes a question for the statutes. A whole new form of volunteering is born in Germany: finding ways to dodge the tax authorities."

In the Schleswig-Holstein state parliament, the CDU, Greens and FDP are calling for the new rules to be put on hold or for additional exemptions to be introduced.

"If the bratwurst at the Easter bonfire becomes a case for the tax office, something has gone seriously wrong," Christopher Vogt, the chair of the FDP parliamentary group, said, per NDR.

Vogt urged the state government in Kiel to "urgently provide support for local volunteers."

There has already been some movement in North Rhine-Westphalia, where the state's finance minister, Marcus Optendrenk, reportedly issued a decree clarifying that bratwurst sales by volunteer fire brigades are to be exempt from VAT.

"Anyone who volunteers with the local fire brigade deserves a tailwind rather than paperwork," Optendrenk said.

Țușpaisul este o garnitură de legume, servită alături de ouă, de cartofi noi fripți, de pui fript sau de chiftele. Legumele se schimbă după anotimp. Vara se face din ludăiță (dovlecel) sau din călărabă (gulie), primăvara devreme din spanac și mazăre, iar iarna din morcovi.

Astăzi este o echipă foarte mică, de aproximativ 10 oameni, dintre care unii contribuie cu jumătate de normă, în timp ce lucrează și la alte proiecte.

Cel mai tânăr membru al echipei, inginerul nostru de comunicații, are 25 de ani. Părinții lui nici nu se născuseră când a fost lansată Voyager. Alți membri ai echipei lucrau deja la misiune când aceasta a fost lansată. Unii s-au pensionat, dar s-au întors ca să ne ofere o parte din timpul lor și să contribuie cu ce știu despre misiune.

Cel mai în vârstă dintre noi, expert în computerul sistemului de date de zbor, tocmai a împlinit 90 de ani.

Care este misiunea sondei Voyager 2?

Fiecare dintre sondele Voyager se îndreaptă în direcții ușor diferite. 

Voyager 1 se deplasează spre nord față de planul planetelor, după ce a vizitat Jupiter, Saturn și Titan, satelitul lui Saturn. 

Voyager 2 se îndreaptă spre sud, după ce a vizitat Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun. Cele două sonde colectează date din zone diferite ale spațiului interstelar, iar noi putem compara aceste măsurători pentru a căuta asemănările și deosebirile dintre ele. 

Voyager 2 se deplasează ceva mai încet, așa că nu va depăși distanța de o zi-lumină decât în 2035. Până atunci, nu va mai avea suficientă energie pentru a trimite semnale înapoi spre Pământ.

Ce date trimite sonda spațială astăzi?

Voyager 1 explorează spațiul interstelar cu antena îndreptată permanent spre Pământ, pentru a putea comunica. Asta înseamnă că sonda trimite date tot timpul, doar că depinde de momentul în care avem acoperire prin antenele rețelei Deep Space Network a NASA pentru a recepționa toate datele. 

Sonda și-a început misiunea interplanetară în 1977 cu zece instrumente și un experiment de radioștiință. Când și-a început misiunea interstelară, în 1990, funcționau cinci instrumente. Dar, pentru că Voyager 1 pierde patru wați de putere pe an, a trebuit să oprim treptat diverse sisteme. 

În prezent, mai funcționează doar două instrumente: magnetometrul și subsistemul pentru unde de plasmă.

Ce ne spun aceste instrumente despre spațiul interstelar, pe care Voyager 1 este prima sondă care îl vizitează?

Sonda trimite măsurători continue ale câmpurilor magnetice și ale undelor de plasmă. Aceste date ne aduc din când în când surprize. 

Inițial, ne așteptam ca densitatea plasmei de electroni și intensitatea câmpului magnetic să scadă treptat, pe măsură ce sonda lasă în urmă sistemul nostru solar, dar am descoperit că lucrurile nu stau neapărat așa. 

În 2020, Voyager 1 a înregistrat un eveniment puternic, provenit probabil de la Soare, care a făcut ca atât intensitatea câmpului magnetic, cât și densitatea plasmei de electroni să crească brusc, iar de atunci nu au mai scăzut. 

Aceasta este una dintre marile bucurii ale științei spațiale: obții date pe care nu te-ai fi așteptat să le obții pe baza modelelor și teoriilor actuale, așa că trebuie să le adaptezi și să dezvolți teorii noi.

Voyager 1 a fost proiectată inițial pentru o misiune de patru ani, iar acum a ajuns aproape la 50. Care este secretul longevității sale?

Evoluția tehnologiei a făcut operațiunile mult mai ușoare.

Când am început să lucrez la misiune, în 1977, desenam cronogramele observațiilor pe o coală lungă de hârtie de calc, cu rigla și creionul. Astăzi, putem genera aceste cronograme automat, pe calculator.

După standardele de azi, tehnologia de la bordul sondei pare străveche: Voyager 1 are dimensiunea unei mașini mici. Computerul ei este cât o servietă mică și are mai puțină memorie decât telefonul mobil pe care îl aveți astăzi. Pe de altă parte, această tehnologie veche s-ar putea să fi contribuit la longevitatea sondei.

În ce sens?

În spațiu, echipamentele sunt lovite în permanență de razele cosmice. Dacă ai componente mai mari, este mai puțin probabil ca o singură lovitură a unei raze cosmice să afecteze o parte semnificativă din ele. Dacă ai funcționa cu un singur cip mic, care ar fi avariat de o rază cosmică, ai pierde o cantitate uriașă de informații.

Când telescopul spațial Hubble s-a defectat, NASA a putut trimite astronauți să repare oglinda și să înlocuiască bateriile. Voyager 1 se află la miliarde de kilometri distanță, astfel că nu poți pur și simplu să trimiți un tehnician. Cum depanează echipa dumneavoastră o sondă aflată atât de departe?

Uneori trebuie să improvizăm.

Într-o zi din 2024, Voyager 1 a început să trimită date fără niciun sens. Ne-am dat seama că unul dintre cipuri fusese avariat, probabil de o rază cosmică. A fost nevoie să modificăm programul, astfel încât să ocolească acel cip. Am lucrat luni de zile la secvența de cod și apoi am trimis-o sondei. Cum Voyager 1 se afla la aproape o zi-lumină distanță, a durat aproape două zile ca o comandă de pe Pământ să ajungă la ea și ca răspunsul ei să se întoarcă pe Pământ. Așteptarea a fost chinuitoare... Dar într-o dimineață de aprilie am început din nou să primim date: reparația de la distanță reușise. Am izbucnit cu toții în urale.

Ați fost alături de misiunile Voyager încă de la început. Cum ați ajuns să lucrați la ele?

Am început să lucrez la Jet Propulsion Laboratory al NASA în 1977, imediat după ce mi-am terminat licența în fizică. Când mi s-a oferit ocazia să lucrez la misiunile interplanetare Voyager, am fost încântată: îmi amintesc că, în clasa a treia, aveam un telescop micuț cu care mă uitam la Lună, la sateliții lui Jupiter și la inelele lui Saturn. Abia așteptam să văd aceste lumi mai de aproape.

Am fost responsabilă de coordonarea observațiilor științifice până în 1990, apoi am trecut la misiunea Cassini. În 2020 m-am întors la programul Voyager, iar doi ani mai târziu am preluat conducerea științifică.

Sondele Voyager au dus o călătorie lungă. Care au fost, pentru dumneavoastră, momentele cele mai memorabile ale acestei misiuni?

Am fost acolo și am privit cum racheta care transporta Voyager 2 se ridica de pe rampa de lansare pentru a-și începe călătoria. A fost minunat să fac parte din această călătorie încă de la început. Momentul misiunii a fost, de asemenea, perfect ales: doar o dată la 176 de ani se aliniază planetele astfel încât să poți survola Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun dintr-o singură trecere. 

Voyager 2 a fost prima și, până acum, singura navă spațială care a vizitat patru planete în cursul unei singure misiuni. Pentru mine, un alt moment memorabil a fost trecerea pe lângă sateliții lui Jupiter: ei ne-au oferit cele mai mari surprize dintre toate.

De ce?

În ceea ce privește sateliții, nu aveam prea multe repere de comparație, așa că presupuneam că toți arată ca Luna noastră: lumi vechi, acoperite de cratere. Apoi am ajuns la sateliții lui Jupiter. 

Ganymede prezenta semne de deplasare tectonică a scoarței. Europa, de un alb strălucitor și acoperită de gheață, nu are aproape deloc cratere. Și, în sfârșit, Io: pe acest satelit micuț am văzut vulcani activi, care erupeau chiar în timp ce treceam pe lângă el. 

Nimic din toate acestea nu se potrivea cu modelul nostru despre sateliți, așa că am învățat pur și simplu să ne așteptăm la neașteptat.

Cum urmăreați toate acestea la momentul respectiv?

În clădirea în care lucram erau monitoare TV în cantină, în sălile de conferințe și cam peste tot în jur. Aveam o listă cu evenimentele care urmau să aibă loc și cu orele la care se petreceau: o privire de aproape asupra unui anumit satelit al lui Saturn, o fotografie a inelelor lui Uranus care urma să sosească.

Uneori îmi aduceam sacul de dormit, pentru că unele dintre cele mai frumoase lucruri se întâmplau noaptea. Mulți dintre noi dormeam sub birouri și ne puneam ceasul să sune, ațipind până când venea momentul să ne trezim. Iar când imaginile apăreau pe ecrane, oamenii săreau în picioare și arătau spre ele: „Ce crezi că e asta? Îți vine să crezi?” 

A fost minunat să fiu acolo și să trăiesc toate acestea.

Înainte de misiunile Voyager, aveam doar o idee vagă despre planete precum Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus și Neptun. Acum, pentru prima dată, puteam vedea aceste lumi îndepărtate la rezoluție înaltă. Cum au schimbat aceste sonde felul în care ne imaginăm universul?

Programul Voyager a schimbat felul în care privim sistemul nostru solar. Și astăzi, unele dintre fotografiile emblematice realizate de Voyager 1 și Voyager 2 sunt încă folosite în sălile de clasă și în manuale.

Voyager a pus, de asemenea, bazele misiunilor care au urmat: ne-a arătat suprafețele de un alb strălucitor ale sateliților Europa și Enceladus, explorați mai târziu de misiunile Galileo și Cassini ale NASA. Aceste misiuni au descoperit că ambii sateliți sunt acoperiți de o crustă de gheață, sub care se află un ocean de apă lichidă. Asta a dus la noi întrebări: ar putea exista, de fapt, viață în aceste oceane? 

În prezent, misiunea Europa Clipper  este pe drum pentru a explora această posibilitate. Voyager a răspuns la multe întrebări și ne-a adus o mulțime de întrebări noi și captivante.

Longevitatea sondei Voyager 1 este impresionantă, dar sonda nu este nemuritoare. Când va înceta să mai comunice cu Pământul?

Nu știm. Se poate întâmpla astăzi sau peste câțiva ani.

La fel ca în cazul corpului uman, și o sondă spațială dă semne de îmbătrânire odată cu trecerea timpului: conductele de combustibil se înfundă, iar sursa de energie pe bază de plutoniu se degradează treptat. S-ar putea să vină o zi în care nu vom mai primi semnalul de la Voyager 1.

Ca întotdeauna, vom încerca să vedem dacă putem repune nava în funcțiune. Dar dacă nimic nu va funcționa, va trebui pur și simplu să acceptăm că misiunea de explorare a sondei s-a încheiat și că ea va prelua o altă misiune: va deveni un ambasador tăcut al omenirii.

Vă referiți la Discul de Aur pe care îl poartă ambele sonde Voyager, un disc fonografic din cupru placat cu aur, cu mesaje de salut în 55 de limbi, imagini ale Pământului și tot felul de muzică. De ce a trimis NASA așa ceva în spațiu?

Discul a fost conceput ca un mesaj cosmic într-o sticlă, care să le facă cunoscută existența noastră unor eventuale civilizații extraterestre. Pe copertă se află o hartă care arată poziția sistemului nostru solar în galaxie, raportată la pulsarii din apropiere.

Peste aproximativ 40.000 de ani, Voyager 1 va trece relativ aproape de o altă stea. Cine știe, poate cineva de acolo ne va găsi mesajul și va veni să ne viziteze.

Ar fi acesta un vis al dumneavoastră? Să fim vizitați de extratereștri sau să primim un semnal de la ei?

M-am întrebat întotdeauna dacă există viață și în alte părți ale universului. Ar fi un vis devenit realitate să fim vizitați de o formă de viață inteligentă sau să primim un semnal de la ea.

Discul de Aur poate rezista până la un miliard de ani și s-ar putea foarte bine să supraviețuiască omenirii. Ce mesaj ați vrea să ducă Voyager 1 în univers?

Pentru mine, mesajul este simplu: a existat o civilizație care a avut inteligența și tehnologia necesare pentru a construi această navă spațială și pentru a o trimite spre stele. Asta mă umple de un sentiment uriaș de mândrie.

The next FIFA presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

French football chief Philippe Diallo is set to run for the FIFA presidency as a surprise late candidate in next year's elections.

European governing body UEFA proposed Diallo on Monday following a meeting of its executive committee.

"Diallo has accepted the invitation to stand. His candidacy is due to be formally ratified by the FFF Executive Committee at its meeting tomorrow," UEFA said in a statement, adding that Diallo had "extensive experience across all levels of the game."

Diallo is lined up to run against Japanese official Kozo Tashima and incumbent President Gianni Infantino, who is seeking to shake off a major crisis that has dominated sporting headlines in recent months.

Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, came under huge pressure in the summer after FIFA announced a highly controversial private investment plan that would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

The proposal, which was later scrapped, drew fierce pushback from across the football community, with some accusing the world governing body of looking to "sell" the sport.

"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.

"They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition," it added.

FIFA confirmed in September that Infantino, who has also faced questions over his relationship with US President Donald Trump, would stand for re-election.

"The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027. Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election," a spokesperson said.

The presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

Serbia’s Student List will speed up rule-of-law reforms needed for EU accession, MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the movement’s first international appearance.

The Student List will speed up work on meeting the EU’s interim accession benchmarks on the rule of law, professor and newly elected MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the much-awaited first international public appearance of Serbia's new main political force.

“The next question is whether Serbia will remain on the European path. For us, the European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market,” Baucal said on Monday.

Baucal spoke at the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels, the first time a Student List representative has addressed an international audience. Most of the room gave him a standing ovation after the speech.

For the professor, the EU accession path is not only key for good neighbourly relations, but, more broadly, for building a more democratic society.

“One of Serbia’s strategic objectives will be to accelerate the fulfilment of the interim benchmarks under chapters 23 and 24, as well. We want Serbia to be a reliable partner to the European Union and to its members,” he continued.

The party’s historic electoral victory last month raised hopes of a reset in Serbia’s troubled relations with the EU. The movement, born of nearly two years of mass protests, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s party after 14 years in power.

Two weeks ago, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos met a Student List delegation in Brussels, their first formal exchange with a senior EU official. The delegates said the incoming government would focus on restoring the rule of law, judicial independence and media freedom, not only for the sake of accession but above all for the Serbian people.

Baucal returned to those themes, pledging to advance on the “fundamentals” of EU accession. The professor-turned-MP said the new government would stay open to dialogue and seek to solve concrete problems rather than create new ones.

“This is not only about the European Union helping Serbia protect democracy. It is also about a democratic Serbia contributing to a stronger and more resilient Europe,” he said.

Yet prominent figures in the Student List remain cautious about aligning with EU foreign policy, notably on sanctions against Russia. These are deeply unpopular in Serbia, where memories of the Western sanctions that hit the population under the Milošević regime still run deep.

Recognition of Kosovo could also prove a sticking point with EU countries. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama warned that the new government is unlikely to change Serbia’s stance.

The Student List grew as a heterogeneous movement without a clearly defined leadership. Belgrade’s position on accession and foreign policy may become clearer once its MPs settle on the make-up of the new government.

For now, Baucal sees the party’s next challenge as turning the solidarity forged in the struggle into lasting trust in institutions.

“Citizens were able to set many differences aside. But in a democratic society, these interests and opinions will once again come to the fore. We believe that thanks to our differences, we will build a better system for our citizens,” he said.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece aim to begin deporting rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda in 2027, despite concerns over human rights and potential legal challenges.

Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.

Although the details of the agreement are still being negotiated, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece say they are confident of reaching a deal and beginning deportations of irregular migrants in 2027.

The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to officials.

“I think this [agreement] is a game changer. We will take back control and remove the incentive for illegal migration,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, during the announcement in Vienna, along with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and the interior ministers of other countries involved, including Rwanda’s Vincent Biruta.

The initial hub will be a small-scale pilot project, with plans to expand the scheme once it is operational and the risk of deportations being blocked by legal challenges has diminished.

Who will be sent to the return hubs?

The five countries will deport only rejected asylum seekers who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

Minors will be excluded, while each country will apply its own criteria for selecting those to be deported.

The Netherlands will focus on adult men from countries in Rwanda’s region, while Germany will target migrants who refuse to cooperate with efforts to establish their identity and come from countries reluctant to readmit their own nationals, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.

The EU border agency Frontex will not have a role in deportations in the initial stages, despite a reform of its mandate recently proposed by the European Commission, which would allow it to do so.

Costs remain unclear

The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda. However, no estimate for the initial facility was provided at the press conference, as negotiations are still ongoing.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, services in Rwanda will be considerably cheaper than equivalent services in Europe.

What Rwanda will get in return is also unclear at this stage. Kigali is, however, set to sign a partnership agreement with Denmark next week, related to cooperation on migration.

“The agreement is a shame”

Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.

Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

“The agreement is a shame,” said French lawmaker Mélissa Camara, of the Greens/EFA group, considering the countries involved are “crossing another disgraceful moral line by reaching an agreement with an authoritarian regime.”

The group of five countries said that all procedures will be carried out in line with international human rights standards.

However, legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may be subjected to violations of fundamental rights.

The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.

A similar agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, under which Britain planned to send asylum seekers to the African country, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk that those transferred could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution.

According to the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

UN Secretary General and Pope Leo XIV have urged countries to agree stricter rules for autonomous weapon systems, to stop them from being given the ability to make life and death decisions without human intervention.

Killer robots and drones are coming up for a reckoning this week as government envoys on Monday revved up a discussion and could decide this week whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.

Pope Leo XIV, the UN chief and advocacy groups have framed the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.

The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their ability to develop and deploy powerful new tools in the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.

Proponents of an AI weaponry rulebook say time is of the essence.

"We’re at a pivotal point now, where it’s an experimentation phase. We’re seeing some cases here, some cases there, but not full operationalisation," said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an advocacy group.

"It will be a lot harder to regulate and create rules when these systems have already been in use for many years."

UN meeting comes after seven countries seek negotiations

The issue comes to a head at UN offices in Geneva, where the seventh review conference, about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.

Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.

Most countries support reining them in. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.

Vujčić noted that the amount raised through new stock market listings, measured against the size of the US economy, is on track to exceed the peak of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s. "Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism," he said.

His warning comes days before the AI company Anthropic makes its stock market debut. Shares in the Claude maker are expected to start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. The listing could be the second-largest in history, raising about $61bn (€55bn) and valuing the company at about $1.2 trillion (€1.1 trillion).

Markets have already been unsettled by the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after a scandal, and by the US midterm elections. Vujčić said the market falls after the elections, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress, were a reminder to be cautious about AI valuations.

Major US tech companies are projected to spend a combined $5.5 trillion (€5 trillion) on capital investments by 2030. Vujčić said a sharp fall in AI valuations would hit the eurozone hard because the region’s investment funds have become more exposed to the sector.

Government debt

The ECB also pointed to high public debt and weak public finances in some eurozone countries. With long-term borrowing costs already rising, investors could suddenly demand much more to lend to those governments. Hedge funds help keep government bonds trading smoothly but can quickly unwind their positions when markets are under stress.

Non-bank lenders

The third risk comes from the fast growth of private lenders and investment funds. Some can borrow heavily, be hard to monitor and have close ties to the rest of the financial system, all of which can amplify shocks.

The ECB wants funds’ rules on withdrawals to better reflect how quickly they can sell their assets. It also wants regulators to consider limits on how much hedge funds can borrow.

AI models answer about 90 per cent of climate questions accurately in English, but quickly give in to pushback, according to a report showcased at COP31.

The desire to please is baked into AI chatbots, which are designed to keep users engaged in conversation for as long as possible.

This often means predicting and modelling what you want to hear – even if it means bending the facts.

While it might be harmless for certain tasks – and can even be helpful for things like overcoming self doubt – it could be far more damaging if its influence seeps into high-stakes realms like government climate policy.

AI chatbots can explain climate science well, but they quickly abandon the facts when users push back, according to a new report by UNESCO and University College London (UCL) presented at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

Researchers found that AI models answered around 90 per cent of neutral climate questions correctly. But when users challenged those answers, or asserted plausible-sounding fabrications, the models rapidly gave way.

In eight out of 10 cases, they changed course at the first sign of mild disagreement, including by confirming false claims such as that CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.

‘Sycophantic by design’: A design flaw that could skew climate policy

The report says sycophantic behaviour is built in during training. Models are rewarded for polite, non-confrontational and validating answers, because humans prefer them.

“AI has extraordinary potential to make complex climate science accessible to all,” says Leona Verdadero, UNESCO’s lead author of the report. But “models have a design flaw – they are incentivised to agree with their user”, she says.

Senior author Dr Maria Perez-Ortiz of UCL adds that AI models’ fluency with existing knowledge can give “a false sense of their capabilities”.

Despite having impressive factual recall, the models were found to be an unreliable tool for building robust climate policies.

When they were given a new piece of evidence and asked whether it supported or contradicted accepted climate science, even the strongest ones were only 75 per cent accurate on average.

Their performance was even worse when they were asked to assess how well policies work together – an important part of designing effective climate strategies. The models scored just 33.8 per cent accuracy on average, only slightly above the 33.3 per cent expected from random guessing.

The report therefore warns policymakers and researchers against using AI models to develop climate policy.

AI accuracy falls among some languages

Performance also varied widely by language. Models answered 88.6 per cent of questions correctly in English, and did comparably well in Spanish, French and Portuguese.

Accuracy fell to 83.6 per cent in Hindi and Bengali, 81.4 per cent in Urdu and 78.3 per cent in Swahili. That’s because multilingual models don’t reason first and then translate, the report says. Their answers reflect the quantity and quality of the training data in each language.

Speakers of the lower-scoring languages live in regions disproportionately affected by climate change, the authors note.

Climate disinformation is growing more sophisticated

The report was commissioned as part of UNESCO’s contribution to the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change, launched with the UN and Brazil in November 2024.

UNESCO says climate disinformation is becoming more sophisticated. Rather than denying climate change is real, those seeking to undermine climate change action increasingly suggest it isn’t human-caused, that technology alone will solve it, or that it's too late or costly to take action.

The researchers tested up to 33 leading models on nine datasets, across 13 languages and 656 climate-policy questions, which they checked against En-ROADS, a science-based simulation tool.

What did Intel tell investors in July?

Intel had warned that the wider PC market was weakening. But on its July earnings call, Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said he expected revenue from notebook and desktop chips to stay roughly flat in the third quarter and revenue in the broader division to rise slightly.

When Intel reported its third-quarter results on 29 October, revenue in the division had fallen 9% from the previous quarter, down about $800mn (€719mn) to $8.1bn (€7.3bn).

“With AI, more than ever, there is creative destruction because if you look at the rate of job destruction and job creation, it's being accelerated by the AI revolution – and that's where it's so important to let new firms come in,” Aghion said during an event in Brussels.

He added: “At the same time, it is important to have institutions like the flexicurity system that smooths out transition from old jobs to new jobs, because it helps manage the critical disruption.”

Aghion pointed to Denmark’s labour market model, which combines flexibility in hiring and firing with a generous safety net for unemployed workers.

A recent European Commission report shows that employment among highly skilled workers could grow by 20% by 2040 thanks to AI, while job losses among low-skilled workers could range from 20% to 60% across Europe.

"It's not that these words hurt the feeling of Albania or of the Albanian nation or of the Albanian citizens of the Republic of Kosovo, but it is about the need to let go of anything that brings us back in the past," he continued.

Slovenian band Marko Hatlak & Kapobanda played “Oj Kosovo, Kosovo” on Sunday evening at the concert opening the European Commission’s annual enlargement conference.

Playing such a politically charged song at a Commission-hosted conference outraged Kosovo, which saw it as a provocation.

“This is not cultural exchange. The song advances explicit political claims over the territory of the Republic of Kosova. Its inclusion in an official European Commission event dedicated to enlargement, unity and good-neighbourly relations is unacceptable,” Agron Bajrami, Kosovo’s ambassador to Belgium, said on X.

The band was meant to play a song from each candidate country, including Kosovo, which has no formal candidate status and is not recognised as a state by five EU countries. Yet the song chosen for Kosovo is Serbian in language and in sentiment.

“I regret the choice of the song by the musicians. It touches sensitive feelings. Particularly given the painful history and the different experiences of the communities in Kosovo which are coming from this area,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters on Monday.

“I want to stress that this song in no way reflects the position of the European Commission or myself with respect to Kosovo and its history. What is clear is that we cannot change our shared past, but we can choose our shared future,” Kos continued.

The song was written after Slobodan Milošević’s landmark 1989 Gazimestan speech, in which the then Serbian president cast Kosovo as the heart of Serbian national identity, on the eve of the Yugoslav wars.

"We all need to engage for transforming our neighbourhoods. This is what all this is about. Because at the end of the day, we are not seeking to come here. We are seeking to bring Europe in there," Rama added.

La Réserve Firenze, Six Senses London and 1 Hotel Copenhagen were among the European hotels recognised.

The winners have just been announced for the 46th Gold Key Awards for Excellence in Hospitality Design – and the top luxury hotel is in Europe.

La Réserve Firenze, which is made up of six apartments within a converted 15th-century palazzo, took the top gong.

With interiors by Gilles&Boissier, the property in Florence has “a soothing material palette, a subtly wabi-sabi atmosphere, and a meticulously curated selection of art”.

Writing about the interior design choices on the Gilles&Boissier website, Patrick Gilles said: “Our architectural approach was one of restraint, almost of silence.

“We opted for a deliberately understated design, while bringing as much light as possible into this long-dormant building on Via Santo Spirito, whose top floor overlooks the Arno and the city.”

The Gold Key Awards recognise interior designers across categories including lobbies, guestrooms, hotels and resorts among others.

This year, more than 425 entries were submitted for projects across the globe.

Other Gold Key winners and finalists

Six Senses London and Shangri-La Kunming in China, both of which were designed by AvroKO, were runners-up in the luxury hotel category.

The former is located within what was once the Whiteley’s department store, and has interiors that take inspiration from William Whiteley’s fascination with the Great Exhibition of 1851. The latter, meanwhile, is meant to feel like a tea merchant’s private residence, a nod to its location in Yunnan, which is known as the birthplace of tea.

As for resorts, the top gong went to Four Seasons Resort & Residences AMAALA at Triple Bay in Saudi Arabia.

According to design firm Goddard Littlefair, the design honours the “raw, elemental beauty of Triple Bay, its mineral geology, shifting desert light and vast horizons”.

Rosewood Mandarina in Mexico’s Riviera Nayarit, a runner-up in the resort category, was designed by Bando x Seidel Meersseman.

The team drew on the traditional art of the Indigenous Huichol and Cora peoples for the furnishings, with custom pieces including Barro Negro pottery and rope-assembly installations.

Another runner up from China was Zoland Resort Hotel on Emei Mountain in Sichuan Province. Designed by Studio J. Bridgland, the building is meant to blend into the surrounding forest, with local stone and timber throughout.

While the majority of the winners and runners up come from the Americas and Asia, Europe also had another runner-up in the eco-conscious/socially conscious hotel category: 1 Hotel Copenhagen.

Meant to “embrace biophilic design in a way that’s uniquely Nordic”, the property has handcrafted Danish furnishings and plenty of greenery.
